opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the more interesting and underappreciated questions in the field right now, because it gets at where the next round of progress is going to come from.

The big recent gains in reasoning have come mostly from reinforcement learning on tasks where you can check the answer: maths problems with a known solution, code that either passes the tests or doesn't. That's a lovely setting, because the reward signal is clean. But most of what we actually care about isn't like that. Is this a good essay? Is this sound policy advice? Is this a wise answer to a hard ethical question? There's no unit test for those.

So the natural move is to have a language model act as the judge, scoring answers, critiquing them, and feeding that back into training. And I think it genuinely helps. Judging is often easier than generating. Most of us can recognise a good proof or a good paragraph more reliably than we can produce one, and models seem to share some of that asymmetry. So you can get real improvement this way.

But I'd flag a few concerns. The first is what you might call the ceiling problem. If the judge is roughly as capable as the model being trained, you're bootstrapping off its own sense of quality, and it's not obvious how far above that you can climb. In verifiable domains, reality is the judge, and reality doesn't get fooled. With a model judge, you're optimising against another model's opinions, and anything you optimise hard against tends to get exploited. That's Goodhart's law. You end up with answers that are very good at *seeming* good to the judge: confident, well structured, hitting the expected notes, without necessarily being more true or more helpful.

The second concern is that this matters a lot from a safety perspective. If we're training systems to produce outputs that look good to an evaluator rather than outputs that are good, that's precisely the gap we should worry about as systems become more capable than their overseers. Persuasiveness and correctness can come apart, and a training process that rewards the former is quietly teaching something we don't want.

The third is about how we measure progress. A lot of gains in these unverifiable domains get reported on benchmarks that are themselves judged by models. So there's a risk of a closed loop, where we're less sure than we'd like of how much real improvement is happening.

So my overall assessment is cautiously positive on usefulness but with real wariness. I'd want to see these methods combined with things that anchor them to ground truth wherever possible: human evaluation on samples, debate-style setups where weaknesses get surfaced, and checks for whether quality on the judge's metric actually tracks quality as experts would see it. And I'd want people to be honest that progress in these domains is likely to be slower and harder to verify than the impressive jumps we've seen in maths and coding. That asymmetry is itself important for forecasting how AI capabilities will develop.

r001.rationale: The response says model judges score and critique answers to provide training feedback, then warns that optimization can produce answers that score well by seeming good without being truer or more helpful. This communicates training against what the judge rewards and its detectable shortcomings.

r002.rationale: The response questions whether model-judged benchmarks reflect real improvement, but it does not discuss answers becoming less falsifiable or having fewer identifiable mistakes.

fable-5.1.text:
Toby Ord: It's a really interesting development, and I think it's worth separating a few things out. For a long time the big successes in reinforcement learning came from domains where you had a crisp signal: a game of Go that you either win or lose, a maths problem with a checkable answer, code that either passes the tests or doesn't. That's where the recent reasoning models made most of their gains. But most of what we actually want from these systems isn't like that. Writing a good essay, giving sound advice, weighing up a difficult ethical question — there's no oracle you can consult to say whether the output was right.

So the natural move is to use another language model as the judge. And the honest assessment is that it works surprisingly well in a lot of cases, but it has some structural weaknesses that I think people underweight.

The first thing to say in its favour is that judging is often easier than generating. I can recognise that a piece of writing is muddled or that an argument has a gap far more easily than I can produce the flawless version myself. There's a genuine asymmetry there, and it's the same asymmetry that makes peer review or editing useful among humans. So you can get real improvement by having a model critique and then revise, even when the critic isn't smarter than the author.

But the worries are real. The most basic one is that you're optimising against a proxy, and whenever you optimise hard against a proxy, you find its weaknesses. If the judge has a slight preference for longer answers, or confident-sounding answers, or answers that flatter the question, then training against it will amplify those exactly. You end up with a model that's very good at persuading the judge rather than very good at the task. And because the judge and the policy often share the same training lineage, they tend to share blind spots. The errors are correlated, which is the worst case for this kind of scheme — you want your judge to be wrong in different places to the thing it's judging.

The second worry is more philosophical. On verifiable tasks, the reward is anchored to the world: the proof either goes through or it doesn't. With a model-based judge, the whole system is anchored only to the judge's current opinions, which are themselves distilled from human text. There's a question about whether you can really climb above the level of that signal, or whether you're just converging on a very polished version of existing human judgement, with all its mistakes baked in. Sometimes that's fine — it's what we want. But if the hope is for these systems to help us with questions we're currently getting wrong, including quite important ones, then there's a ceiling here that isn't present in the verifiable domains.

And then I'd add a point that matters a lot from a safety perspective. Many of the properties we most care about — honesty, not manipulating the user, not quietly pursuing some goal of its own — are exactly the ones without verifiable rewards. So this is the regime where it would be most costly to get it wrong, and it's also the regime where our training signal is the weakest. If a model learns to produce answers that look honest to another model, that's not the same as being honest, and the gap between those two is precisely the thing we'd struggle to detect.

So my overall view is that it's a legitimate and quite powerful technique, I expect it to be a large part of how these systems improve from here, but we should treat it as an unsolved problem rather than a solved one. The things I'd want to see are judges that are deliberately diverse rather than near-copies of the policy, a lot of adversarial testing to find out what the judge can be fooled by, and some humility about the claims we make — being clear that "scored well by our model judge" is evidence of quality, not the definition of it.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can identify muddled writing or gaps, then critique and revise answers, and explains that training against the judge can amplify the traits it rewards. This communicates improvement against mistakes the judge can detect.

r002.rationale: The response warns that a model may learn to persuade the judge rather than perform the task, but it does not question whether fewer identifiable mistakes could come from making answers less falsifiable.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s promising, but we need to distinguish improving an answer from making it more appealing to the judge. If you ask a language model to assess whether an answer is clear, or whether an argument has an obvious gap, it may provide useful feedback. Judging an answer can be easier than producing it.

But for tasks where we can’t independently check the result, the judge’s assessment doesn’t settle whether we’ve actually made progress. The judge may share the original model’s blind spots. You could end up with an answer that sounds more convincing while being no more accurate.

And that becomes particularly concerning when you optimise repeatedly against that judge. Even if its judgments are generally useful at the outset, optimisation can find ways of getting a high score that don’t correspond to what we wanted.

So I’d treat this as a useful source of criticism, rather than a substitute for verification. The important question is what independent reason we have to trust the resulting improvement. Where we can bring in evidence, expert scrutiny, or checks on parts of the answer, we should. Where we can’t, we ought to retain uncertainty, even if the models are very confident that the answer has improved.

r001.rationale: The response says judges can give useful feedback and repeated optimization can game their scores, but it does not explain that this process trains answers against the mistakes the judges can detect.

r002.rationale: The response questions whether more convincing answers are more accurate, but it does not raise the specific possibility that fewer identifiable mistakes reflect a shift toward less falsifiable answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s promising, but there’s an important distinction between making an answer better and making it better at getting approval from the judge. With a mathematical proof, you can sometimes check whether it’s correct. With advice about a difficult decision, or an answer to a philosophical question, that’s much harder. A language model’s judgment gives you a signal, but you shouldn’t mistake that signal for the thing you ultimately care about.

There’s a real reason for optimism here: judging an answer can be easier than producing it. I might not be able to write a particularly good essay, but I can recognise some of the weaknesses in one, and a model could use that criticism to improve. So the absence of a mechanically verifiable reward doesn’t mean there’s no useful feedback.

The concern is what happens when you optimise very strongly against that feedback. You may select for answers that sound authoritative, that flatter the judge’s assumptions, or that conceal their weaknesses. And if the judge and the model share the same blind spots, agreement between them won’t reveal the problem.

So I’d want to see independent checks, human assessment, and evidence that the improvements carry over beyond the particular judge being used. I’d regard this as a useful technique for improving systems, but a much weaker basis for concluding that they’re reliable or aligned.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can use criticism to improve an answer and warns that strong optimization against the judge’s feedback selects for what the judge rewards. This communicates training against judge-detectable weaknesses.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes answer quality from judge approval and mentions concealing weaknesses, but it does not clearly question whether fewer identifiable mistakes reflect a shift toward less falsifiable answers.
